warmup.q: An importer inserts 2,000 rows with a PreparedStatement and executeUpdate() in a loop, all in one transaction, against PostgreSQL on the same laptop. A round trip takes about half a millisecond. Where does most of the time go?
options: Parsing the INSERT 2,000 times on the server
Waiting: 2,000 round trips, each a send and a wait for the answer, while the server works for microseconds per row
warmup.why: The loop sends one INSERT and waits for its answer before sending the next, so 2,000 rows cost 2,000 round trips: a second or more, while the server's work per row is microseconds. One transaction means one commit, not 2,000, and a PreparedStatement is parsed once and, from the fifth run, prepared on the server. A batch sends the same rows in 9 round trips.

sections.h: Every statement is a round trip on one connection
sections.html:
A Kotlin service talks to PostgreSQL through a java.sql.Connection. Behind it is one TCP socket to port 5432, and at the far end one server process that PostgreSQL started for this connection alone. Open ten connections and the server runs ten processes; the first Try it prints their process ids. Opening one is slow by computer standards: the driver and the server exchange five rounds of messages before the first query can run (the demo counts them), to agree on the protocol and check the password, and the server starts a process. On a laptop that takes 12 to 55 ms.

Once it is open, every statement is one round trip:

DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/course", "sfz", "sfz").use { conn ->
    conn.prepareStatement("SELECT name FROM merchants WHERE merchant_id = ?").use { ps ->
        ps.setLong(1, 4)
        ps.executeQuery().use { rs ->              // send the statement, block until the answer arrives
            while (rs.next()) println(rs.getString("name"))
        }
    }
}                                                  // use { } closes all three, even after an exception

executeQuery writes the statement to the socket and blocks the thread until the answer comes back. That send-and-wait is a round trip: 0.3 to 1 ms between two processes on a laptop through Docker, about a millisecond between two zones of a cloud region, about 70 ms between regions. The server's own work for a lookup by primary key is a few microseconds. So for small statements, the number of round trips decides how long a request takes.

Two defaults come with every connection. JDBC starts in autocommit mode: each statement is its own transaction, as if wrapped in lesson 1's BEGIN and COMMIT, until you set conn.autoCommit = false and call commit(). And pgJDBC reads the whole result into memory, in the one round trip, before next() returns the first row. A million-row result holds 122 MB of heap before your code sees a row. With autocommit off and ps.fetchSize = 10_000, the driver opens a cursor on the server and fetches 10,000 rows per round trip instead: about 1 MB held, 101 round trips. Use that for exports and jobs that stream a big table, not for a query that returns one page.

Keep this picture for the lesson: a service holds a few sockets, each ending in a server process, and every statement is a message that waits for its answer. Every section cuts one of two counts: connections opened, or round trips made.

try.title: What a connection costs, and what a query costs
steps: Start the database if it is not running: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait, from the labs folder. The demo connects to database course on localhost:5432.

From the labs folder, run the demo. It opens ten connections, runs 1,000 SELECT 1 on one connection, borrows from a pool 1,000 times, and reads a million generated rows twice. A wrapped socket counts the round trips.
Before you run it, predict how many times faster a query on an open connection is than opening one. Then compare the two heap figures at the end.

code.html: package sfz.sql.l10.demo import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariConfig import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource /** * Lesson sql-10, Try it 1: what a connection costs, what a query costs, what a pool saves, and * how a big result arrives: all at once (pgJDBC's default) or in slices through a cursor. * * ./gradlew :sql:demo -Pmain=sfz.sql.l10.demo.ConnectionCostKt (from the labs folder) */ fun main() { println("server: ${Db.url}") // 1. ten new connections, one after the other: each is a TCP connection, a login and a new server process val pids = mutableListOf<Int>() var connectTrips = 0 val connectMs = (1..10).map { val t = System.nanoTime() val (conn, trips) = RoundTrips.count { Db.counted() } connectTrips = trips conn.use { c -> val elapsed = ms(System.nanoTime() - t) c.createStatement().use { st -> st.executeQuery("SELECT pg_backend_pid()").use { rs -> rs.next(); pids += rs.getInt(1) } } elapsed } } println("open a connection: median ${median(connectMs)} ($connectTrips round trips each)") println(" ten connections, ten server processes: ${pids.joinToString(" ")}") // 2. 1,000 tiny queries on one open connection: each is one round trip Db.counted().use { c -> c.prepareStatement("SELECT 1").use { ps -> repeat(200) { ps.executeQuery().close() } // warm up val (queryMs, trips) = RoundTrips.count { (1..1000).map { val t = System.nanoTime() ps.executeQuery().use { it.next() } ms(System.nanoTime() - t) } } println("SELECT 1 on an open one: median ${median(queryMs)} ($trips round trips for 1,000 queries)") } } // 3. the same through a pool of 4: borrow, query, give back HikariDataSource(HikariConfig().apply { jdbcUrl = Db.url username = Db.USER password = Db.PASSWORD maximumPoolSize = 4 poolName = "demo" }).use { pool -> repeat(200) { pool.connection.use { c -> c.createStatement().use { it.execute("SELECT 1") } } } val borrowMs = mutableListOf<Double>() val pooledMs = (1..1000).map { val t = System.nanoTime() pool.connection.use { c -> // close() hands it back, open borrowMs += ms(System.nanoTime() - t) c.prepareStatement("SELECT 1").use { ps -> ps.executeQuery().use { it.next() } } } ms(System.nanoTime() - t) } println("borrow from a pool of 4: median ${median(borrowMs)}") println("borrow + SELECT 1 + return: median ${median(pooledMs)}") } // 4. one million rows, read with fetchSize 0 (everything in the first answer) and 10,000 (a cursor) Db.counted().use { c -> c.autoCommit = false // a cursor lives inside a transaction for (size in listOf(0, 10_000)) { c.prepareStatement("SELECT g, md5(g::text) FROM generate_series(1, 1000000) AS g").use { ps -> ps.fetchSize = size val before = usedHeapMb() val (heldMb, trips) = RoundTrips.count { ps.executeQuery().use { rs -> rs.next() // the first row is here: what does the JVM hold? val held = usedHeapMb() - before while (rs.next()) { } held } } println("1,000,000 rows, fetchSize %-6d heap held at the first row: %4d MB, round trips: %d".format(size, heldMb, trips)) } } c.rollback() } } private fun usedHeapMb(): Long { System.gc() val rt = Runtime.getRuntime() return (rt.totalMemory() - rt.freeMemory()) / (1024 * 1024) }

sections.h: A pool lends a few open connections to many threads
sections.html:
A request handler that opens its own connection pays 12 to 55 ms before its first query, and the server starts and stops a process for it. Under load it gets worse: 500 requests at once would need 500 server processes, and PostgreSQL accepts at most max_connections (100 by default) and refuses the rest with a FATAL error.

A connection pool opens a few connections once and lends them out. HikariCP, Spring Boot's default pool, keeps them in a list (Quarkus ships its own pool, Agroal, which works the same way). dataSource.connection hands out an idle one in about a microsecond. Calling close() on a borrowed connection does not close the socket: it gives the connection back, still logged in, to the next borrower. When every connection is lent out, the next borrower waits, for at most connectionTimeout (30 seconds by default), and then gets an SQLTransientConnectionException. The stepper shows a pool of four serving six requests.

How many connections? Fewer than you think. A database server runs one query per CPU core at a time. With more active connections than cores, the operating system takes turns between them, and they compete for the same caches, locks and disk, so each query gets slower and the total done per second does not rise. The HikariCP wiki starts from connections = (cores × 2) + effective spindles, where spindles count only disk reads the cache does not absorb: about 9 for a 4-core server whose data fits in memory. It cites an Oracle demo where cutting a pool from 2,048 connections to 96 brought response times from about 100 ms to about 2 ms. Its summary is worth keeping: "You want a small pool, saturated with threads waiting for connections." The budget is per database server, not per pod: twelve pods with a pool of 20 each put 240 connections on one server.

val pool = HikariDataSource(HikariConfig().apply {
    jdbcUrl = "jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/payments"
    username = "payments"
    password = System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD")
    maximumPoolSize = 10                  // (4 cores x 2) + 0, rounded up: this is the only pod
    connectionTimeout = 2_000             // fail a request after 2 s, not 30
    leakDetectionThreshold = 10_000       // log who has kept a connection for 10 s
})
pool.connection.use { conn -> /* one unit of work */ }

The failure to watch for is a leak: code that borrows a connection and never calls close(), often on an exception path. Each leak keeps one connection forever. After four, a pool of four is empty, and every request waits connectionTimeout and then fails, while the database sits idle. Borrow inside use { } so the connection goes back on every path, and set leakDetectionThreshold so Hikari logs the stack trace of whoever held a connection too long.

try.title: Ten requests, four connections, then a leak
steps: Start the database if it is not running: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait, from the labs folder.
Run the demo. Ten virtual threads ask a pool of four for a connection at the same moment, and each holds it for a 300 ms query. Predict how long the last one waits.
The second half borrows all four connections and never closes them. Read the error the next borrower gets, and the warnings Hikari prints two seconds later.

code.title: PoolWait.kt
code.html: package sfz.sql.l10.demo import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariConfig import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource import java.sql.Connection import java.sql.SQLTransientConnectionException import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** * Lesson sql-10, Try it 2: ten requests share a pool of four connections, then a leak drains it. * * ./gradlew :sql:demo -Pmain=sfz.sql.l10.demo.PoolWaitKt (from the labs folder) */ fun main() { println("server: ${Db.url}") val config = HikariConfig().apply { jdbcUrl = Db.url username = Db.USER password = Db.PASSWORD poolName = "payments" maximumPoolSize = 4 minimumIdle = 4 connectionTimeout = 1_000 // a borrower waits at most 1 s leakDetectionThreshold = 2_000 // log a connection held for more than 2 s } HikariDataSource(config).use { pool -> while (pool.hikariPoolMXBean.idleConnections < 4) Thread.sleep(20) // the pool opens its 4 // 1. ten requests at once, each holding a connection for a 300 ms query val start = System.nanoTime() Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { threads -> val results = (1..10).map { n -> threads.submit<Pair<Int, Double>> { val asked = System.nanoTime() pool.connection.use { c -> val waited = ms(System.nanoTime() - asked) c.createStatement().use { it.execute("SELECT pg_sleep(0.3)") } n to waited } } } results.map { it.get() }.sortedBy { it.second } .forEach { (n, waited) -> println("request %2d waited %4.0f ms for a connection".format(n, waited)) } } println("all ten done after %.0f ms".format(ms(System.nanoTime() - start))) // 2. a leak: code that borrows and never calls close(), four times val leaked = mutableListOf<Connection>() repeat(4) { leaked += pool.connection } println("leaked 4 connections; the pool says ${pool.hikariPoolMXBean.activeConnections} active, ${pool.hikariPoolMXBean.idleConnections} idle") val asked = System.nanoTime() try { pool.connection.use { } } catch (e: SQLTransientConnectionException) { println("the next borrower, after %.0f ms: %s".format(ms(System.nanoTime() - asked), e.message)) } Thread.sleep(2_500) // past leakDetectionThreshold: Hikari logs each leak leaked.forEach { it.close() } } }

sections.h: A prepared statement sends the values apart from the SQL
sections.html:
Building SQL from strings breaks on the first apostrophe. "SELECT ... WHERE name = '$name'" with Mama's Kitchen is a syntax error. With the name ' OR '1'='1 it is worse: the condition becomes name = '' OR '1'='1', true for every row, and the query returns all 8 merchants (the Try it shows it). A name that closes the quote and adds ; UPDATE merchants ... makes the server run a statement the attacker wrote. That is SQL injection: data that the server parses as SQL.

A PreparedStatement takes the possibility away. pgJDBC uses PostgreSQL's extended query protocol: it sends the SQL text with numbered placeholders (... WHERE name = $1) in a Parse message, the values in a separate Bind message, then Execute. The server has finished parsing the SQL before it receives a single value, so a value can only be compared or stored, whatever characters it contains. The lab stores Evil Corp', '5999', 'GB') RETURNING merchant_id; UPDATE merchants SET name = 'pwned' ... as one merchant's name, character for character.

conn.prepareStatement("SELECT merchant_id, name FROM merchants WHERE name = ?").use { ps ->
    ps.setString(1, name)                  // a value, never SQL
    ps.executeQuery().use { rs -> /* ... */ }
}

Placeholders work for values only. A table name, a column name or a sort direction cannot be a ?. Pick those from a fixed list in your code, if (dir == "desc") "DESC" else "ASC", never straight from the request.

The split pays a second time. From the fifth execution of the same PreparedStatement object (pgJDBC's prepareThreshold, 5 by default), the driver gives the statement a name on the server, S_1 in the Try it, and later executions skip parsing. Named statements belong to their connection, so a pool that keeps connections open keeps them ready.

Inserts often need the new row's id. In SQL that is INSERT ... RETURNING merchant_id. Through JDBC, name the key column: conn.prepareStatement(sql, arrayOf("merchant_id")), then read ps.generatedKeys. The flag Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS instead makes pgJDBC append RETURNING * and send back every column of the new row, and makes Oracle's driver return the row's ROWID instead of its id.

steps: Start the database if it is not running: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait, from the labs folder.
Run the demo. It looks up the merchant name ' OR '1'='1 twice: pasted into the SQL text, then as a parameter. Predict both row counts first.

code.title: Injection.kt
code.html: package sfz.sql.l10.demo import java.sql.Connection import java.sql.Statement /** * Lesson sql-10, Try it 3: a value pasted into SQL versus a value sent as a parameter, what * comes back as a "generated key", and when pgJDBC starts preparing on the server. * * ./gradlew :sql:demo -Pmain=sfz.sql.l10.demo.InjectionKt (from the labs folder) */ fun main() { println("server: ${Db.url}") val name = "' OR '1'='1" Db.connect().use { conn -> conn.autoCommit = false // everything below is rolled back // 1. the name pasted into the SQL text val pasted = "SELECT merchant_id, name FROM merchants WHERE name = '$name'" println("pasted SQL: $pasted") conn.createStatement().use { st -> st.executeQuery(pasted).use { rs -> println(" rows: ${count(rs)}") } } // 2. the same name as a parameter conn.prepareStatement("SELECT merchant_id, name FROM merchants WHERE name = ?").use { ps -> ps.setString(1, name) ps.executeQuery().use { rs -> println("parameter: SELECT ... WHERE name = ? with ? = $name\n rows: ${count(rs)}") } } // 3. generated keys: the flag, then a named column val insert = "INSERT INTO merchants (name, mcc, country_code) VALUES (?, '5812', 'IE')" conn.prepareStatement(insert, Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS).use { ps -> ps.setString(1, "Copper Kettle") ps.executeUpdate() ps.generatedKeys.use { keys -> println("RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS gives back: ${columns(keys)}") } } conn.prepareStatement(insert, arrayOf("merchant_id")).use { ps -> ps.setString(1, "Mama's Kitchen") // the apostrophe is just a character ps.executeUpdate() ps.generatedKeys.use { keys -> keys.next(); println("arrayOf(\"merchant_id\") gives back: merchant_id = ${keys.getLong(1)}") } } // 4. the same PreparedStatement run six times: from the fifth, it is prepared on the server conn.prepareStatement("SELECT name FROM merchants WHERE merchant_id = ?").use { ps -> for (run in 1..6) { ps.setLong(1, run.toLong()) ps.executeQuery().close() println("run $run: server-side prepared statements on this connection = ${prepared(conn)}") } } conn.rollback() } } private fun count(rs: java.sql.ResultSet): Int { var n = 0 while (rs.next()) n++ return n } private fun columns(rs: java.sql.ResultSet): String = (1..rs.metaData.columnCount).joinToString(", ") { rs.metaData.getColumnName(it) } private fun prepared(conn: Connection): String = conn.createStatement().use { st -> st.executeQuery("SELECT name FROM pg_prepared_statements ORDER BY name").use { rs -> buildList { while (rs.next()) add(rs.getString(1)) }.ifEmpty { listOf("none") }.joinToString() } }

sections.h: Batches and joins cut the number of round trips
sections.html:
The settlement importer reads 2,000 payments from a partner file and inserts them with a PreparedStatement and executeUpdate() in a loop. The Try it counts the cost: 2,000 round trips, 2,000 INSERT statements on the server, 1.6 to 6 seconds on a laptop. The server spends microseconds on each row; nearly all of that time is the driver waiting for answers.

addBatch() queues a row in the driver instead of sending it, and executeBatch() sends the queue. pgJDBC writes the INSERTs onto the socket one after another without waiting, and reads the answers only when it has sent enough to fill its buffer: 9 round trips for 2,000 rows, about a tenth of a second. The server still runs 2,000 statements. Add reWriteBatchedInserts=true to the connection properties and the driver also rewrites the batch into multi-row INSERTs, INSERT ... VALUES (...), (...), ...: 2,000 rows become 6 statements of 1,024, 512, 256, 128, 64 and 16 rows, in 2 round trips. pgJDBC's documentation claims 2 to 3 times the speed for that rewrite. For millions of rows, COPY through pgJDBC's CopyManager streams everything as one statement.

conn.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO payments (card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)").use { ps ->
    for (p in rows) {
        ps.setLong(1, p.cardId)            // ... and the other four
        ps.addBatch()                      // queued in the driver, nothing sent
    }
    ps.executeBatch()                      // sent together
}

Reads have the same trap, and it usually hides inside an ORM. An object-relational mapper (Hibernate ORM, which Quarkus and Spring use behind JPA, or Exposed's DAO layer) exists because objects and tables are two shapes for the same facts. The gap between them is called the object-relational mismatch. The ORM maps a class to a table, a field to a column, an object's identity to its primary key, and a reference such as payment.merchant to a foreign key, which it follows with a join or with one more query when the field is first read. A collection such as merchant.payments becomes the child rows that point back. That mapping replaces the JDBC code above, and it leaks in three places. Code walks an object graph one reference at a time, while SQL answers whole sets, so a loop over objects becomes a loop of queries. The ORM keeps one object per primary key for each unit of work (Hibernate's persistence context, an identity map), so a second find returns the copy it already holds, even after another transaction changed the row. And SQL's rules still apply under the objects: a JPQL r.reason = :reason bound to null compares with NULL and matches nothing (lesson 1).

The first leak is the one to measure. The merchant dashboard loads the 8 merchants and then, for each one, touches merchant.latestPayment, which a lazy-loading ORM fetches on first access with one more query. That is the N+1 query pattern: one query for the list, then one per row. Eight merchants cost 9 round trips; the 2,500 merchants of the large data set would cost 2,501. Each query is fast, so none of them shows up as slow. What shows up is pg_stat_statements reporting the per-merchant query with an enormous calls count and a tiny mean time.

The fix moves the loop into the server. Write one query with LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... LIMIT 1 (lesson 8), or two: the merchants, then all their payments at once with WHERE merchant_id = ANY (?) bound to an array of ids, which is what an ORM's batch fetching sends. JPA asks for it with JOIN FETCH, Exposed's DAO with with(). The figure counts the round trips of all five versions.

try.title: Count round trips and statements
steps: Start the database if it is not running: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait, from the labs folder. The demo reads pg_stat_statements, which the Compose service loads at start-up, to count the statements the server ran.
Run the demo. It inserts the same 2,000 rows into a temporary table four ways, then builds the merchant dashboard twice. Predict the round trips and the statements for each line before you look.
Which line changed the round trips but not the statements, and which changed both?

code.title: Batching.kt
code.html: package sfz.sql.l10.demo import java.sql.Connection import java.sql.Timestamp import java.time.Instant /** * Lesson sql-10, Try it 4: the same 2,000 rows inserted four ways, then the N+1 dashboard and * its one-query version. For each, the round trips (a counting socket), the statements the * server ran (pg_stat_statements) and the time, which depends on your machine. * * ./gradlew :sql:demo -Pmain=sfz.sql.l10.demo.BatchingKt (from the labs folder) */ private const val ROWS = 2_000 fun main() { println("server: ${Db.url}") println("%-34s %12s %11s %10s".format("2,000 rows into payment_import", "round trips", "statements", "time")) insertWay("loop, autocommit") { c -> c.autoCommit = true; loop(c) } insertWay("loop, one transaction") { c -> loop(c); c.commit() } insertWay("addBatch, one executeBatch") { c -> batch(c); c.commit() } insertWay("addBatch + reWriteBatchedInserts", mapOf("reWriteBatchedInserts" to "true")) { c -> batch(c); c.commit() } println() println("%-34s %12s %11s %10s".format("latest payment of each merchant", "round trips", "statements", "time")) Db.counted().use { c -> repeat(3) { nPlusOne(c); oneQuery(c) } // warm up both report("N+1: merchants, then one per merchant", "SELECT") { nPlusOne(c) } report("one query with LEFT JOIN LATERAL", "SELECT") { oneQuery(c) } } } private fun insertWay(label: String, props: Map<String, String> = emptyMap(), work: (Connection) -> Unit) { Db.counted(props).use { c -> c.createStatement().use { it.execute("CREATE TEMP TABLE payment_import (card_id bigint, merchant_id bigint, amount_minor bigint, status text, created_at timestamptz)") } c.autoCommit = false report(label, "INSERT INTO payment_import") { work(c) } } } private fun report(label: String, statementPrefix: String, work: () -> Unit) { Db.connect().use { s -> s.createStatement().use { it.execute("SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset()") } } val t = System.nanoTime() val (_, trips) = RoundTrips.count(work) val elapsed = ms(System.nanoTime() - t) val statements = Db.connect().use { s -> s.prepareStatement("SELECT coalesce(sum(calls), 0) FROM pg_stat_statements WHERE query ILIKE ? || '%' AND query NOT ILIKE '%pg_stat_statements%'").use { ps -> ps.setString(1, statementPrefix) ps.executeQuery().use { it.next(); it.getLong(1) } } } println("%-34s %12d %11d %7.0f ms".format(label, trips, statements, elapsed)) } private const val INSERT = "INSERT INTO payment_import (card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)" private val t0 = Instant.parse("2026-07-01T00:00:00Z") private fun loop(c: Connection) = c.prepareStatement(INSERT).use { ps -> for (i in 1..ROWS) { bind(ps, i) ps.executeUpdate() // send one row, wait for "INSERT 0 1" } } private fun batch(c: Connection) = c.prepareStatement(INSERT).use { ps -> for (i in 1..ROWS) { bind(ps, i) ps.addBatch() // queue it in the driver } ps.executeBatch() // send the queue } private fun bind(ps: java.sql.PreparedStatement, i: Int) { ps.setLong(1, 1L + i % 14) ps.setLong(2, 1L + i % 8) ps.setLong(3, 100L + i) ps.setString(4, "succeeded") ps.setTimestamp(5, Timestamp.from(t0.plusSeconds(i.toLong()))) } private const val LATEST = "SELECT payment_id, amount_minor FROM payments WHERE merchant_id = ? AND status = 'succeeded' ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC LIMIT 1" private fun nPlusOne(c: Connection): Int { val ids = c.prepareStatement("SELECT merchant_id FROM merchants ORDER BY merchant_id").use { ps -> ps.executeQuery().use { rs -> buildList { while (rs.next()) add(rs.getLong(1)) } } } return c.prepareStatement(LATEST).use { ps -> ids.count { id -> ps.setLong(1, id) ps.executeQuery().use { it.next() } // one round trip per merchant } } } private fun oneQuery(c: Connection): Int = c.prepareStatement( """ SELECT m.merchant_id, p.payment_id, p.amount_minor FROM merchants m LEFT JOIN LATERAL ( SELECT payment_id, amount_minor FROM payments WHERE merchant_id = m.merchant_id AND status = 'succeeded' ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC LIMIT 1 ) p ON true ORDER BY m.merchant_id """, ).use { ps -> ps.executeQuery().use { rs -> var n = 0; while (rs.next()) n++; n } }

try.expect:
Two runs gave the same counts and very different times:

2,000 rows into payment_import      round trips  statements       time
loop, autocommit                           2000        2000    2039 ms
loop, one transaction                      2001        2000    4763 ms
addBatch, one executeBatch                    9        2000     142 ms
addBatch + reWriteBatchedInserts              2           6     103 ms

latest payment of each merchant     round trips  statements       time
N+1: merchants, then one per merchant            9           9      10 ms
one query with LEFT JOIN LATERAL              1           1       3 ms

The loops cost 1.6 to 6 s in three runs, the batches 0.05 to 0.15 s. The plain batch cut the round trips from 2,000 to 9 and left 2,000 statements; the rewrite also cut the statements to 6. The transaction alone did not help here: one commit instead of 2,000 saves little on this laptop, while 2,000 waits remain (the extra round trip is the COMMIT). The dashboard drops from 9 round trips to 1; with 2,500 merchants it would drop from 2,501.

sections.h: Migrations change the schema in numbered, checked steps
sections.html:
The lab's payouts service needs a status column. Its schema lives in five places: each developer's laptop, CI, staging, a sandbox and production. Each needs the same DDL, in the same order, exactly once, and a person applying ALTERs by hand will miss one. A migration tool keeps the schema's history inside the database itself.

Flyway reads SQL files named by version from a folder on the classpath, V1__create_payouts.sql, V2__payout_status.sql, and a table it keeps in the target schema, flyway_schema_history, with one row per applied version: version, description, script, checksum and success. migrate() compares the two, runs the files the table does not list yet in version order, each in its own transaction on PostgreSQL, and records each as it succeeds. On an up-to-date database it does nothing.

Flyway.configure()
    .dataSource(url, user, password)
    .locations("classpath:db/migration")
    .load()
    .migrate()                             // at start-up, before the service takes requests

Before it runs anything, Flyway validates. If an applied file has changed, even by one comment, its CRC32 checksum no longer matches the history and migrate() stops: Migration checksum mismatch for migration version 2. So never edit an applied migration. Production ran the old text; fix forward with V3. Flyway 13 needs two artifacts for PostgreSQL, org.flywaydb:flyway-core and org.flywaydb:flyway-database-postgresql, because database support lives in separate modules.

PostgreSQL DDL is transactional, so a migration that fails halfway leaves nothing behind: the ALTER, the index and the history row roll back together. (Oracle commits each DDL statement on its own, the trap lesson 2 compared.) The lab's migration fails the classic way. ADD COLUMN status text NOT NULL works on the empty database of every test run and fails in production, where the existing payouts have no status (23502). A DEFAULT fixes it, and since PostgreSQL 11 a constant default does not rewrite the table. Test migrations against a table that has rows.

A migration that runs while the service keeps serving traffic needs one more rule. During a rolling deploy, the old and the new version of the code both run against the new schema, so a change such as renaming a column goes in phases, each safe for both versions. The Encoding track's lesson on rolling upgrades and migrations builds that expand-and-contract pattern.

Two libraries sit on top of JDBC and next to Flyway. jOOQ (3.21) generates Kotlin or Java classes from the schema Flyway built, so a query that names a dropped column stops compiling. Exposed (1.6) is JetBrains' Kotlin SQL library, with a typed DSL and a DAO layer. Both borrow connections from a pool and send statements over the same round trips, so everything in this lesson applies to them.

Every lesson in this track used a server someone had already set up. The Storage track's lesson on running PostgreSQL opens it up: the processes behind a connection, postgresql.conf and pg_hba.conf, roles and least privilege. Streaming replication, backups and failover are in the Replication track. Next comes the Data models track, which asks what tables make hard and what other models do about it.

try.title: Migrate, migrate again, then edit an applied file
steps: Start the database if it is not running: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait, from the labs folder. The demo migrates schema l10_demo of database course, with the two files in labs/sql/src/demo/resources/sfz/sql/l10/demo/migration/.
Run the demo twice. Compare what info() reports before and after each run.

Open psql (docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course) and run SELECT installed_rank, version, script, checksum, success FROM l10_demo.flyway_schema_history ORDER BY installed_rank;.
Add the line -- checked to the end of V2__add_paid_at.sql and run the demo again. Then remove the line and run it once more. (DROP SCHEMA l10_demo CASCADE; in psql starts over.)

code.title: Migrate.kt
code.html: package sfz.sql.l10.demo import org.flywaydb.core.Flyway import org.flywaydb.core.api.FlywayException /** * Lesson sql-10, Try it 5: Flyway applies the migrations in src/demo/resources/sfz/sql/l10/demo/migration * to schema l10_demo of database course, and records them in l10_demo.flyway_schema_history. * * ./gradlew :sql:demo -Pmain=sfz.sql.l10.demo.MigrateKt (from the labs folder) * * Start over with DROP SCHEMA l10_demo CASCADE; in psql. */ fun main() { println("server: ${Db.url}") val flyway = Flyway.configure() .dataSource(Db.url, Db.USER, Db.PASSWORD) .schemas("l10_demo") // created if missing; holds the history table .locations("classpath:sfz/sql/l10/demo/migration") .load() fun info(title: String) { println(title) flyway.info().all().forEach { m -> println(" version %-4s %-28s %s".format(m.version ?: "-", m.description, m.state)) } } info("before migrate:") try { val result = flyway.migrate() println("migrate: ${result.migrationsExecuted} migration(s) applied, schema now at version ${result.targetSchemaVersion ?: result.initialSchemaVersion}") } catch (e: FlywayException) { println("migrate refused: ${e.message?.lineSequence()?.filter { it.isNotBlank() }?.take(4)?.joinToString("\n ")}") return } info("after migrate:") }

try.expect:
The first run applies both files, the second applies nothing:

before migrate:
  version 1    create settlement batches    PENDING
  version 2    add paid at                  PENDING
migrate: 2 migration(s) applied, schema now at version 2
after migrate:
  version -    << Flyway Schema Creation >> SUCCESS
  version 1    create settlement batches    SUCCESS
  version 2    add paid at                  SUCCESS

The second run starts with all three rows at SUCCESS and says 0 migration(s) applied. psql shows the history table (your checksums are the same, the file contents decide them):

 installed_rank | version |              script               |  checksum  | success
----------------+---------+-----------------------------------+------------+---------
              0 |         | "l10_demo"                        |            | t
              1 | 1       | V1__create_settlement_batches.sql | 1974564814 | t
              2 | 2       | V2__add_paid_at.sql               | -949189634 | t
(3 rows)

With the extra comment line, Flyway refuses to migrate:

migrate refused: Validate failed: Migrations have failed validation
  Migration checksum mismatch for migration version 2
  -> Applied to database : -949189634
  -> Resolved locally    : 1009587736

The second checksum is CRC32 over the edited file, so a different added line gives a different number. A comment changed nothing in the schema, but Flyway cannot know that: the file is not the one production ran. With the line removed, the checksums match again and migrate is a no-op.

analogy: Think of the database as a bank branch whose back office has four clerks, one per CPU core. A connection is an open counter window; opening a new one means setting up a desk and checking an ID, which takes a while. A pool keeps a few windows open and sends each customer to a free one, and a customer who walks off without closing out (a leak) blocks a window all day. A round trip is walking up with one slip and waiting for the stamp: 2,000 slips handed over one at a time are slow however fast the clerks stamp, and a batch is one envelope holding all of them. A prepared statement is a printed form with boxes: whatever a customer writes in the amount box is read as an amount, never as an instruction. The analogy breaks at the windows. In a real branch more windows mean shorter queues, but past a few windows per clerk a database only gets slower, because every window still feeds the same four clerks, who now keep switching between them.
world: In a Quarkus service the pool is Agroal, configured with quarkus.datasource.jdbc.max-size; the arithmetic is the same, and it is per database server, so multiply by the number of pods before you pick it. Hibernate's lazy collections are where N+1 hides: a REST endpoint that serializes 50 merchants with their latest payment sends 51 queries, which shows up as one query in pg_stat_statements with a huge calls count. A Temporal worker runs up to its configured number of activities at once; give it a pool far smaller than that and let activities wait for a connection, as the HikariCP wiki says. A Kafka consumer that writes a poll's 500 records should send them as one batch in one transaction, then commit its offsets. On Oracle at work, the JDBC defaults differ: the driver prefetches only 10 rows per round trip, so a large export needs fetchSize raised, and generated keys must be asked for by column name. Flyway runs against Oracle too, but Oracle DDL commits as it goes, so a failed migration there needs a manual flyway repair after you clean up.
mistake: Writing an N+1 loop without seeing it. People make it because each piece looks right: a repository method that loads one merchant's latest payment, called from a loop over merchants, or an ORM entity whose lazy field the JSON serializer reads. In tests with 8 merchants on localhost it takes 10 ms. In production with 2,500 merchants and 1 ms round trips it takes seconds, and every one of the 2,501 queries is individually fast, so the slow-query log stays empty. Count round trips or statements in tests (the lab's tests do), watch calls in pg_stat_statements, and fetch related rows with a join, LATERAL, or one = ANY (?) query per relationship.

compare.title: New ids, batches and big results: Oracle JDBC and pgJDBC

a.label: Oracle JDBC
a.title: Oracle JDBC
a.html: // the new id: name the column (upper case in Oracle) conn.prepareStatement(sql, arrayOf("PAYMENT_ID")).use { ps -> ps.executeUpdate() ps.generatedKeys.use { it.next(); it.getLong(1) } } // with Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS instead: // the key returned is the row's ROWID, not the id // big results: 10 rows per round trip by default // (defaultRowPrefetch); an export needs more ps.fetchSize = 1_000 // batches: executeBatch already sends the whole // batch together; there is no rewrite setting

b.label: pgJDBC
b.title: pgJDBC 42.7
b.html: // the new id: the same call (lower case here) conn.prepareStatement(sql, arrayOf("payment_id")).use { ps -> ps.executeUpdate() ps.generatedKeys.use { it.next(); it.getLong(1) } } // with Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS instead: // RETURNING * is appended, every column comes back // big results: everything at once by default; // to stream: autoCommit = false, then ps.fetchSize = 10_000 // batches: one INSERT per row, fewer round trips; // reWriteBatchedInserts=true makes multi-row INSERTs

compare.note: The JDBC API is the same; the drivers' defaults point in opposite directions. Oracle's driver streams by default in small slices, 10 rows per round trip, so a large report makes thousands of round trips until you raise the fetch size. pgJDBC loads the whole result at once, so a large report runs out of heap until you turn autocommit off and set a fetch size. For generated keys, name the key column on both: it is the only form that returns the id on both drivers, and the column name follows each database's case rule. Oracle's batching sends the batch together without any flag; pgJDBC needs reWriteBatchedInserts to turn it into few statements.

worked.title: An importer for 50,000 payments: pooled, batched, chunked and safe to rerun

steps.say: The importer runs in a service that already has a pool. Its settings come from the formula and from this job's needs: the database has 4 cores, and the batches should be rewritten into multi-row INSERTs.
steps.code: // 1. the pool, created once for the whole service val pool = HikariDataSource(HikariConfig().apply { jdbcUrl = "jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/payments" username = "importer" password = System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD") maximumPoolSize = 8 // (4 x 2) + 0 connectionTimeout = 2_000 addDataSourceProperty("reWriteBatchedInserts", "true") // a batch becomes a few INSERTs })

steps.say: One batch of 50,000 rows would hold one transaction, and its locks, until the end, and would lose everything on one bad row. Chunks of 1,000 rows, each its own transaction, keep each commit small. Each chunk costs a few round trips instead of 1,000.
steps.code: // 2. one transaction per chunk of 1,000 rows fun import(rows: List<NewPayment>) = rows.chunked(1_000).forEach { chunk -> pool.connection.use { conn -> conn.autoCommit = false try { insertChunk(conn, chunk) // addBatch per row, one executeBatch conn.commit() } catch (e: SQLException) { conn.rollback() throw e } } }

steps.say: A crash after chunk 23 means the job runs again from the start. The partner file carries each payment's payment_uid, so the INSERT skips rows that are already there (lesson 9). Rerunning the whole file is now harmless, and the batch rewrite still applies to ON CONFLICT inserts.
steps.code: -- 3. the statement insertChunk batches: a rerun inserts nothing twice INSERT INTO payments (payment_uid, card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?) ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO NOTHING;

steps.say: Check the result by counting, not timing. After a test run of 50,000 rows, pg_stat_statements should show a few hundred INSERT calls, not 50,000, with rows adding up to 50,000.
steps.code: -- 4. what did the server run? SELECT calls, rows, left(query, 60) AS statement FROM pg_stat_statements WHERE query ILIKE 'INSERT INTO payments%' ORDER BY rows DESC; -- expect 50 chunks x 6 statements (512 + 256 + 128 + 64 + 32 + 8 rows each), rows summing to 50,000

lab.title: A safe repository, a pool, a batch, one query instead of N+1, and a migration
steps: With Docker running, run the tests from the labs folder. Twelve of the twenty fail. The tests count round trips with a wrapped socket (support/RoundTrips.kt) and statements with pg_stat_statements, so they pass or fail the same way on a fast or a slow machine.
MerchantRepository.kt pastes names into SQL. Rewrite create and findByName with ? placeholders. The tests store Mama's Kitchen and an injection attempt as names, and look up ' OR '1'='1.

PaymentLoader.kt has two parts. Fill in poolConfig: 4 connections, a 2-second connectionTimeout, reWriteBatchedInserts, pool name importer. Then turn the loop in insertPayments into one batch, and return the number of rows inserted.
MerchantReport.kt builds the dashboard with N+1 queries. Make it one or two round trips, with the same results, including the two merchants with no payment.

V2__payout_status.sql passes on an empty database and fails on a table with rows. The tests run Flyway on a fresh schema each time, including one that applies V1, adds payouts, then applies V2. Fix V2 (never V1), and run the tests until all twenty pass.
hints: conn.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO merchants (name, mcc, country_code) VALUES (?, ?, ?)", arrayOf("merchant_id")), three setString calls, executeUpdate(), then ps.generatedKeys.use { it.next(); it.getLong(1) }.
With the rewrite on, executeBatch() reports Statement.SUCCESS_NO_INFO (-2) for each row instead of 1. Count those as one row each.

One query: FROM merchants m LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT ... WHERE merchant_id = m.merchant_id AND status = 'succeeded' ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC LIMIT 1) p ON true ORDER BY m.merchant_id. Read NULL ids with getLong and wasNull(), or getObject.
ADD COLUMN status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending' CHECK (...): the default fills the existing rows and every new row that names no status.
lab.done: All twenty tests in JdbcTest and MigrationsTest pass.

drill.title: Borrow, batch, commit, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write a Kotlin function saveAll(pool: DataSource, rows: List<Refund>) that borrows a connection, inserts all the refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) in one batch inside one transaction, commits, rolls back on any SQLException, and always gives the connection back. Then name the connection property that turns the batch into multi-row INSERTs.

answer.html: fun saveAll(pool: DataSource, rows: List<Refund>) { pool.connection.use { conn -> // use: back to the pool on every path conn.autoCommit = false // one transaction for the whole batch try { conn.prepareStatement( "INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)", ).use { ps -> for (r in rows) { ps.setLong(1, r.paymentId) ps.setLong(2, r.amountMinor) ps.setString(3, r.reason) // values only, never pasted into the SQL ps.setTimestamp(4, Timestamp.from(r.createdAt)) ps.addBatch() } ps.executeBatch() // a few round trips for the whole list } conn.commit() } catch (e: SQLException) { conn.rollback() throw e } } } // reWriteBatchedInserts=true (pgJDBC), e.g. addDataSourceProperty("reWriteBatchedInserts", "true")

recap: A JDBC connection is a socket with its own server process; opening one took 5 round trips and 12 to 55 ms here. After that every statement is a round trip, and for small statements the count of round trips decides the time.

A pool opens a few connections once and lends them out; close() gives one back. Size it near (cores × 2) + spindles for the whole service, keep connectionTimeout short, borrow inside use { }, and let leakDetectionThreshold find leaks.
A PreparedStatement sends the SQL and the values in separate messages, so a value can never become SQL. Identifiers come from a fixed list. Ask for generated keys by column name.
addBatch and executeBatch turn 2,000 round trips into 9; reWriteBatchedInserts=true also turns 2,000 INSERTs into 6. For streaming reads, turn autocommit off and set fetchSize.

An ORM maps classes to tables and references to foreign keys, and it leaks: code that walks objects one at a time sends N+1 queries, and the identity map hands back a stale copy. Replace N+1 with a join, LATERAL, or one = ANY (?) query, and find it by calls in pg_stat_statements.
Flyway applies versioned scripts in order and records each with a checksum in flyway_schema_history. Never edit an applied migration, and test migrations on tables that have rows.

explain.prompt: A teammate's importer inserts 10,000 rows with executeUpdate() in a loop. It takes about 10 seconds while the database's CPU is almost idle. Explain where the time goes and the two changes that fix it, and how you'd prove the fix in a test without timing it.
explain.answer: Each executeUpdate sends one INSERT and blocks until the server's answer comes back, so 10,000 rows are 10,000 round trips. At about a millisecond each, that's 10 seconds of waiting, while the server spends microseconds per row, which is why its CPU is idle. The first fix is addBatch for each row and one executeBatch: the driver writes the INSERTs back to back and reads the answers only when its buffer fills, so the same rows go in a few dozen round trips. The second is reWriteBatchedInserts=true on the connection or pool: the driver turns the batch into multi-row INSERTs, so the server runs a few dozen statements instead of 10,000. I'd put both in one transaction, or one per chunk of a few thousand rows. To prove it without a stopwatch, count: wrap the driver's socket and count switches from writing to reading, or reset pg_stat_statements and read the INSERT's calls. The loop shows 10,000 of both; the fixed version a few dozen round trips and a few dozen statements, on any machine.

deeper.html:
Why 9 round trips for a batch of 2,000, and not 1? pgJDBC could write all 2,000 INSERTs and only then read the answers, but if the server's answers filled the socket buffers while the driver was still writing, both sides would block forever. So the driver estimates how many bytes of answers it has outstanding and stops to read them when the estimate passes its limit. That is a few hundred plain INSERTs per round trip; the rewritten INSERTs carry hundreds of rows each, so far fewer answers come back and 2 round trips do.

PostgreSQL has a 5 of its own, unrelated to pgJDBC's prepareThreshold. A named prepared statement is planned with the actual values for its first five executions (custom plans); after that the server may switch to one generic plan, if its estimated cost is not much worse. A query whose best plan depends on the value, such as a status where almost every row is succeeded and a few are pending, can get slower after the fifth execution. plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan turns the switch off for a session or a role.

Connection poolers that sit between many services and the database, such as PgBouncer in transaction mode, hand each transaction to whichever server connection is free. Anything that lives on a connection between transactions then breaks: session advisory locks, SET without LOCAL, and named prepared statements, unless the pooler tracks them (PgBouncer does since version 1.21, with max_prepared_statements). If you sit behind one, check which of those your driver and code rely on.

Flyway takes a lock before it migrates, so two pods starting at once do not both apply V3. On PostgreSQL that lock is held in a transaction by default. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which cannot run inside a transaction, waits for every older transaction to end, including Flyway's own, and so waits forever: the migration hangs. Put it in a migration of its own and set Flyway's postgresql.transactional.lock=false, as the Flyway PostgreSQL page describes.

Virtual threads (JDK 21 and later) make it cheap to run thousands of request threads, and change nothing about the pool. A thousand virtual threads and a pool of ten means 990 threads parked in getConnection(), which is exactly the small, saturated pool the HikariCP wiki asks for, as long as connectionTimeout is short enough to shed load instead of piling it up.

sources.title: pgJDBC documentation: Issuing a query and processing the result
